READING PASSAGE 1
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1
on pages 2 and 3.
Making copies
The earliest forms of copying
The process of copying is essential to any civilisation, since it is the means by which culture
is spread. The oldest ‘copier’ created by humankind was language. Through language it is
possible to express an idea and pass it on. The second ‘copier’ to be created was writing.
Five thousand years ago, the Sumerians, who were inhabitants of what is now Iraq,
transposed spoken words into marks on clay tablets. Later, writing was done on papyrus,
which was similar to paper and was derived from a type of grass found in the Nile River delta
of Egypt. Writing expanded the human network that language had created, and freed
copying from the chain of face-to-face, living contact. It made ideas permanent, portable and
endlessly reproducible.
However, until Johann Gutenberg invented the printing press in the mid-1400s using
moveable type, reproducing anything, including books, generally meant writing words out
again by hand. Even with Gutenberg's printing press it still wasn't possible to take a
document that already existed, feed it into a press and run off facsimiles.
The first copying machine
The first true mechanical copier was manufactured in 1780, when James Watt, who is better
known as the inventor of the modern steam engine, created the copying press. Watt's
copying press is no longer used and few people today know how it worked. A user took a
document freshly written in a unique ink, placed a moistened sheet of translucent paper
against the inked surface and squeezed the two sheets together in the press, causing some
of the ink from the original to penetrate the second sheet, which could then be read by being
turned over and read from the back. Watt's copying press was standard in offices for over a
hundred years, but was displaced, at the end of the 1800s, by a combination of two
inventions: the typewriter and carbon paper.
Modern copying machines
Among the first modern copying machines was the Thermo-Fax, which was introduced in
1950 by the American corporation 3M. It made copies by shining infrared light through an
original document and a sheet of paper that had been coated with heat-sensitive chemicals.
Competing manufacturers were soon marketing other copying machines using similar
technologies. These machines and their successors were commercially successful as there
were no other practical means of reproducing documents, but they had serious drawbacks.
All made copies that were costly, smelled bad, were hard to read, didn't last long, and
tended to curl up.
A remarkable office copier
None of those machines are still manufactured today. They were all made obsolete by a
radically different machine, which was developed by an obscure American photographic-
supply company. That company, founded in 1906 as the Haloid Company, is today known as
the Xerox Corporation. Xerography was initially conceived by Chester Carlson, a patent
attorney, in 1937. Unusually for a modern inventor, Carlson did not work with colleagues and

made his discovery by himself. He offered his invention to more than 20 major corporations,
but they all turned him down, thereby passing up the opportunity to manufacture what has
been described as, 'the most successful product ever marketed in America’. The Haloid
Company did invest in Carlson's idea in 1947, and introduced its first xerographic copier, the
Model A, in 1949. However, the machine was incredibly difficult to operate and was a
commercial failure. Over the next decade, Haloid scientists and Carlson made improvements
to the design until the company came up with the Haloid Xerox 914. This was a machine that
made sharp, permanent copies on ordinary paper. It was a huge breakthrough.
The process employed by the Xerox 914 was based on two natural phenomena which were
already well known in physics: that materials of opposite electrical charges attract, and that
some materials become better conductors of electricity when exposed to light. The Xerox
914 involved a six-step process to transfer an image from one surface to another using these
phenomena. The machine employed what is called a photo-receptor, a powder known as the
toner, and heat to melt the toner into a permanent pattern.
The effects of the new copier
Behaviour-changing technological shifts are sometimes incomprehensible until after they
have occurred. Xerox machines represented such a shift, and had a sweeping impact.
Secretaries were the largest users of the Xerox 914. The ease of using it meant they
produced far more copies than ever before. The technology created the demand that
ultimately sustained production of the machine. In 1955, four years before the Xerox 914, the
world made about 20 million copies; in 1964, five years after the initial marketing of the
Xerox 914, the world made nine and a half billion, almost all using xerography. Five hundred
and fifty billion copies spewed out of machines in 1984. By 2004, the number had climbed to
the trillions, and this figure continues to increase today.
Chester Carlson — a remarkable man
As a result of his original idea, Chester Carlson eventually became very wealthy. His
royalties amounted to something like a 16th of a US cent for every Xerox copy made
worldwide until 1965. Despite this, he was never motivated by money and didn't develop a
taste for possessions. He never owned a second home or a second car. People who knew
him casually seldom suspected that he was rich or even well-to-do. He spent the last years
of his life quietly giving away his fortune to charities, and living a relatively simple life.
